To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the dust and gas temperatures are coupled in molecular cloud cores with densities above ∽3 × 10 4 cm−3 and (2) the gas temperature in the absence of a heat source is expected to decrease with decreasing density in such cores.

(1) in molecular cloud cores, gas and dust are coupled in the regime where CO and other molecular species de- pletes onto dust grains, (2) the gas temperature decreases towards the centers of such cores, (3) the mass of cores which can be supported by thermal pressure alone is small, and (4) the temperature in cores in high pressure clouds like Orion is expected to be higher than in low pressure clouds like Tau- rus.

(1) the gas temperature in pre-protos- tellar cores with densities below ∼3 × 10 4 cm 3 is well coupled to the dust temperature and (2) the gas temperature is higher than the dust temperature at higher densities where CO and many other molecules are expected to be frozen out.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and stability of pre-protostar cores in the presence of radiation fields.
the structure of pre-protostar cores in molecular clouds, and the stability of these cores in external radiation field.
the structure and evolution of molecular clouds, and in particular the pre-stellar cores which form the building blocks for star formation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structure of pre-protostars is not very sensitive to the exact details of heating and cooling processes, but that one needs to consider these in a consistent manner.
the structure of molecular cloud cores can be computed in a self-consistent fashion by taking into account deviations from isother- mality.

the thermal equilibrium in molecular clouds depends sensitively on the radiation field and pressure, and that the structure of cores in such clouds is determined by a complex interplay between thermal and magnetic pressures, turbulence and cosmic ray heating.
The main takeaway from our work is that

one should not use isothermal models for the structure of molecular cloud cores, but instead should use models which take into account the coupling between the gas and dust temperature and its dependence on the radiation field and pressure.
in order to understand the structure of molecular clouds, it is necessary to take into account both the effects of external radiation and the coupling between gas and dust temperatures.
the structure and stability of cores are very different from those obtained in the isothermality approximation.
